extracted.intended_audience: UAS manufacturers and OEMs, component suppliers, UAS service providers, cybersecurity professionals, industry stakeholders, legal and policy practitioners, and members of the public invited to submit comments to BIS
extracted.subtask_short: ANPRM comments on UAS ICTS supply chain
extracted.subtask_description: Provide public comments and technical information to BIS in response to an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) about transactions involving information and communications technology and services (ICTS) integral to unmanned aircraft systems (UAS), focusing on national security risks, definitions, mitigation measures, authorizations, and economic impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: E.O. 13873 undue or unacceptable risks criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To fall within the scope of the prohibition under E.O. 13873, the Secretary must determine that the ICTS transaction: (1) involves ICTS designed, developed, manufactured, or supplied by persons owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of a foreign adversary; and (2) (A) poses an undue risk of sabotage to or subversion of the design, integrity, manufacturing, production, distribution, installation, operation, or maintenance of information and communications technology or services in the United States; (B) poses an undue risk of catastrophic effects on the security or resiliency of United States critical infrastructure or the digital economy of the United States; or (C) otherwise poses an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are collectively referred to as 'undue or unacceptable risks.' The Secretary may design or negotiate mitigation measures to allow otherwise prohibited transactions to proceed and may promulgate rules establishing when transactions involving particular technologies may be categorically prohibited or excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'unmanned aircraft systems' (UAS)
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS requests comment on definitions of UAS to use in potential rulemaking, including ITA's definition (air vehicles and associated equipment that do not carry a human operator, but instead are remotely piloted or fly autonomously), FAA's definition (an unmanned aircraft and associated elements required for safe operation in the national airspace), and EAR's UAV definition (aircraft capable of initiating and sustaining controlled flight without humans on board).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS is inclined toward ITA's definition because it identifies specific components and systems integral to UAS (aircraft, remote pilot station, command-and-control link, payloads) and would include UAS subsystems (control stations, CNPC links, payloads, flight termination systems, recording capabilities, software/AI, remote updates). Comments should address which definition(s) are most appropriate and any amendments needed to better address national security risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of ICTS components integral to UAS
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS preliminarily identifies ICTS integral to UAS that might be included in mitigation/prohibition measures: (1) onboard computers responsible for processing data and controlling UAV flight; (2) communications systems including flight controllers, transceiver/receiver equipment, proximity links such as GNSS sensors, and flight termination equipment; (3) flight control systems (exteroceptive and proprioceptive sensors); (4) ground control stations (GCS) or systems including handheld flight controllers; (5) operating software including network management software; (6) mission planning software; (7) intelligent battery power systems; (8) local and external data storage devices and services; (9) artificial intelligence (AI) software or applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS solicits comment on whether additional components should be identified as integral and whether there are commonly used definitions and standard capabilities for each component (e.g., American Security Drones Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks associated with UAS (data exfiltration and remote access)
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS identified data exfiltration and remote access/control as the two primary areas of risk associated with transactions involving foreign adversary ICTS integral to UAS technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIS asks whether there are other risks or contributing factors it has not considered, and which specific sectors or elements of critical infrastructure are most at risk if UAS technology is compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of foreign adversaries and nexus requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any regulated transactions must have a sufficient nexus to a foreign adversary. E.O. 13873's implementing regulations at 15 CFR 791.4 currently include China (including Hong Kong), Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and Venezuelan politician Nicolás Maduro as foreign adversaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should address how to define foreign adversary nexus and whether other countries/entities should be included or excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of legal/regulatory frameworks of foreign adversaries
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS examines foreign laws (e.g., China's National Intelligence Law, Cybersecurity Law, PIPL; Russian laws) that could compel companies to provide data or cooperate with security services, increasing risk that companies subject to those laws could be directed to compromise U.S. ICTS or UAS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents should provide evidence and analysis of how foreign legal frameworks create tangible risks and examples of exploitative behavior (e.g., forced cooperation, pre-positioned backdoors, compelled updates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation measures and technical controls
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS solicits input on mechanisms to mitigate risks posed by foreign adversary ICTS integral to UAS, such as design requirements, machine learning controls, implementation standards and protocols, cybersecurity firmware/software inputs, manufacturing integrity protections, protection systems and procedures, or prohibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should describe specific mitigation technologies, standards, or operational practices, and evaluate their effectiveness in reducing undue or unacceptable risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization process for otherwise prohibited transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS seeks comment on whether to create a process for the public to request specific authorization to engage in certain transactions involving foreign adversary ICTS integral to UAS by demonstrating that parties have implemented measures adequately mitigating the risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should address what evidence, certifications, or controls would be sufficient to obtain authorization and the structure/timing of such an authorization process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope focus for BIS regulation (platforms, components, capabilities, or end-user sectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS requests comment on the appropriate focus of any regulations: UAS platforms and subcomponent technology, UAS capabilities, or UAS end-user sectors (including entities providing services using UAS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide arguments and data for preferred scope—e.g., component-level rules vs. platform-level prohibitions—and impacts on mitigation feasibility and enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry standard definitions and capabilities for specific ICTS components
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there commonly used definitions and standard capabilities for each of the identified ICTS components (onboard computers, communications systems, flight control systems, GCS, operating software, mission planning software, intelligent batteries, data storage devices/services, AI software)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide references to industry standards, specifications, or norms and explain how those could be used in any BIS rule to identify covered technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data storage, retention, transfer, and disposition practices
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS asks where data captured by UAS is stored (onboard and offboard), how long it is stored, whether data-related services equipment is located outside the United States, and what standard data disposition policies or procedures exist following account termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should describe typical data flows, storage locations (including cloud providers), retention periods, disposition practices, and implications for national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: UAS companies' access to and review of U.S. persons' data
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS asks what standard policies or procedures govern UAS companies' and UAS OEMs' review of or access to data generated by, owned by, or otherwise associated with U.S. persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide descriptions of contractual, technical, and operational controls that restrict or permit access by vendors, OEMs, cloud providers, or foreign entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data privacy protections and industry standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there industry standard policies or procedures establishing how UAS companies must or should protect the privacy of data generated by, owned by, or otherwise associated with U.S. persons?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of existing privacy frameworks, audits, certification programs, or contractual safeguards and comment on their sufficiency for national security concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cybersecurity measures, authentication, and controls for data protection
rubrics_metrics.description: What cybersecurity measures, authentication, or controls do UAS service providers and other companies supporting the UAS supply chain use to mitigate risks surrounding data collection, access, storage, processing, and exfiltration?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail technical measures (encryption at rest/in transit, secure boot, code signing, authentication protocols), organizational practices, and supply-chain security practices used in industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of UAS into critical infrastructure and sensitivity assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: How are UAS integrated in critical infrastructure sectors, and which integrated UAS services are particularly unique or sensitive such that a disruption would create a gap for the sector?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify sectors and describe how UAS use-case sensitivity (e.g., long-duration flights, BVLOS, heavy payloads) affects potential national security risk and mitigation priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensor roles and standards in critical industries
rubrics_metrics.description: What role do specific remote sensing ICTS components (imagery, 3D, acoustic, particle, RF sensors, proximity/navigation sensors, electromagnetic sensors, inertial sensors) serve for data collection by UAS, and are there standard requirements or aftermarket customization options?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide technical descriptions of sensor capabilities, standard performance metrics, and common modification practices with implications for risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and practices for data sharing relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the standard practice for data sharing relationships between UAS companies and individuals or entities within the United States, including agreements with cloud providers that may require exclusive or prioritized use of a cloud service's network infrastructure?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of contractual arrangements and the purposes for which data is shared beyond primary collection objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party integration and supplier identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Who are the third parties that commonly provide payloads and component parts (sensors, payloads, cameras) for integration into UAS production, and which of these third parties are owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of a foreign adversary?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify suppliers, ownership, incorporation and physical locations, and provide factual support where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-U.S. third-party ICTS component provenance and assembly locations
rubrics_metrics.description: What ICTS components (other than payloads) are made by non-U.S. third parties for incorporation into UAS? Where are these component parts made, where are UAS assembled, and who typically incorporates these components?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide supply chain mapping (tier 1/2/3 suppliers), manufacturing and assembly sites, and which actors are responsible for integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for cybersecurity updates (software/firmware/AI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who provides and is responsible for cybersecurity updates to software, firmware, and AI software and applications for component parts integrated into UAS (e.g., sensors, cameras, payloads)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe typical practices: OEM push updates, third-party vendor updates, user-applied patches, and how update authority and mechanisms create risk or mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OEM ability to terminate functionality and best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: In what instances, and how, would OEMs be able to terminate functionality of a UAS (denial of service)? What are the standards and best practices governing the ability of OEMs to terminate functionality? Are there instances where a third party could remotely deny service independently of the OEM? What are best practices for reinstating full operability?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide technical and policy practices governing forced updates, kill-switches, geofencing/no-fly zones, recovery procedures, transparency around update mechanisms, and recommendations to prevent misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls and procedures governing AI use in UAS
rubrics_metrics.description: What controls or procedures govern or should govern the use of AI in UAS?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe testing, validation, explainability, model provenance, supply chain controls for ML models, runtime safeguards, and standards that could reduce the risk of adversarial manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry standard policies for UAS communication protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there industry standard policies or procedures that govern how UAS communicate, what kinds of information UAS can communicate, with what they can communicate, and which components enable, store, or analyze these communications?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify existing standards (protocols, CNPC link standards, encryption, authentication), governance bodies, and gaps relevant to national security regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Component independence: sensors communicating independently of OS
rubrics_metrics.description: To what extent can individual sensors and components communicate independently from the UAS Operating System (OS)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain architectures where components have direct connectivity, the risks posed by independent communication channels, and mitigation techniques to control independent communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical connectivity range and offline data handling
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the physical range of connectivity for UAS systems for commercial use? Where is data stored on the physical UAS and off the UAS? How long is data stored, and how do operators secure data when not connected to the internet?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide empirical ranges for common connectivity technologies (Wi‑Fi, Bluetooth, cellular), typical on-device storage capacities and retention practices, and offline encryption/back-up practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard assessments, audits, or evaluations of data privacy policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any standard assessments, audits, or evaluations, internal or external, of UAS companies' data privacy policies related to any data generated by, owned by, or otherwise associated with U.S. persons?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of audit frameworks, third-party assessments, compliance regimes, or industry certifications and comment on their adequacy for national security review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls for integration of third-party payloads and components into software/OS/AI
rubrics_metrics.description: How do UAS OEMs or operators integrate payloads and related components from third parties into their software, OS, and AI software and applications?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe validation, sandboxing, code review, supply chain assurance, and testing processes used during integration and in ongoing maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for exemptions or exclusions of end users from prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Which, if any, categories or classifications of end users should BIS consider excluding from any prohibitions on transactions involving foreign adversary ICTS integral to UAS because such transactions would not pose an undue or unacceptable risk?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide justification and proposed categories (e.g., emergency responders, certain academic research) and safeguards to limit misuse of exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of ICTS transactions requiring specific authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: For what categories of ICTS transactions relating to UAS should BIS require a specific authorization before the transaction is permitted in the United States?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose criteria for categorization (component criticality, end use, foreign nexus) and the evidentiary showing necessary for an authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for authorizations and electronic certifications with BIS
rubrics_metrics.description: Please comment on potential requirements for authorizations and certifications for industry participants (assemblers, manufacturers, dealers, sellers) filed electronically with BIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address what information should be required, timing, confidentiality handling (BCI), and whether certain attestations or third-party validations should be mandated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification/validation process and role of third-party testing
rubrics_metrics.description: What certification or validation process should be implemented to validate mitigation actions taken? Should third‑party testing and evaluation occur, and at what stage should testing occur to validate mitigation actions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend testing regimes, accredited labs, stages (design, manufacturing, post-deployment), and documentation needed to demonstrate mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic impact, anticompetitive and data privacy cost–benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS seeks comment on potential economic impacts of regulation: anticompetitive effects, data privacy and protection impacts to U.S. businesses or the public, other economic impacts, and how to minimize potential costs to U.S. businesses or the public (including international respondents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide empirical evidence, market-share analyses, cost estimates, and suggested provisions to mitigate negative economic effects while addressing security risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing integrity and supply chain security
rubrics_metrics.description: BIS solicits input on manufacturing integrity (the security of the manufacturing process to ensure no foreign adversary manipulation), supply chain manipulation risks, and the potential for backdoors or malicious functionality introduced during manufacturing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe provenance tracking, secure manufacturing practices, tamper-evident processes, supplier vetting, and standards that can demonstrate manufacturing integrity.
